n: A second heavenly council scene, deliberately echoing the first. The repetition signals that a second, harder test is coming.
The Lord asks the same question and receives the same answer. Satan is still roaming, still looking for weakness.

f.w: From going to and fro in the earth

n: The Lord points to Job again: he still holds on to his integrity, even though Satan urged God to ruin him for no reason. Job’s suffering was not a punishment for sin.

f.g: Keeps his wholeness and faithfulness intact.
For no reason — the same Hebrew word as “for nought” in Job 1:9.

n: Satan replies with a proverb: “Skin for skin” — a person will give up anything to save his own life. Losing possessions and even children wasn’t enough, he claims.

f.g: Probably a trading proverb: a man will trade anything for his own skin.

n: Strike his body, Satan says, and he will curse you. His accusation is that human faith is ultimately selfish.
The Lord allows it, but sets a firm limit: Job’s life must be spared.
Satan strikes Job with painful sores covering his whole body, from the soles of his feet to the top of his head.

f.g: Painful, inflamed skin sores; the exact disease is unknown.

n: Job sits in the ash heap outside town, scraping his sores with a piece of broken pottery. The richest man in the East now sits in the garbage dump.

f.g: Likely the town’s ash and rubbish heap, where outcasts sat.

n: Job’s wife, who has also lost all her children and wealth, speaks in despair: Why hold on? Curse God and die. Her words echo exactly what Satan predicted.

f.w: Dost thou still retain thine integrity?

f.g: Again the Hebrew politely says “bless,” meaning “curse.”

n: Job gently rebukes her for speaking like a godless person, then asks: should we accept only good from God and never trouble? He still does not sin with his words.

f.g: Hebrew nabal — morally foolish, godless, not merely unintelligent.

f.w: shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?

f.g: Here meaning trouble or misfortune, not sin.

n: Three friends from different lands arrange to come comfort him. Their names and homelands suggest wise men from the regions east of Israel.

f.g: From Teman in Edom, known for its wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7).
Possibly descended from Shuah, a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2).
From Naamah, a place of uncertain location.

n: Seeing him from a distance, they barely recognize him. They weep aloud, tear their robes, and throw dust in the air over their heads in mourning.
They sit silently with him on the ground for seven days and nights. Their silent presence was their best comfort — later, their words will hurt more than help.

f.g: The traditional period of mourning for the dead (Genesis 50:10).

f.w: none spake a word unto him
